lede: The tasks people bring to AI models account for 23 percent of US wages, pay has stayed within its usual range while the mix of jobs has shifted more than in any three years since 2013, and 42 percent of new degrees are in fields that lead to the most exposed jobs.
meaning: The tasks people bring to AI models are paid about a quarter of all the wages in the United States, while pay across the skills behind them has moved no further over the last three years than in an ordinary stretch of the record, so these models already reach a wide share of paid work and there is no sign yet that employers pay for those skills differently.

The reading that stands out is the mix of work: over the last three years employment has moved toward jobs that draw on arts and humanities by more than in any three-year stretch since 2013, although a record of thirteen years produces a shift that size by chance about one time in eleven, and the same test was passed in 2020, when the pandemic reshuffled employment, so the next release of the wage tables will show whether it holds.

What employers ask for moved before the models did: within occupations, job ads named the tasks the models can do less often from 2020 to the third quarter of 2022, and the release itself added a step of 2.6 standard errors against the 5.4 needed to stand out from an ordinary month.

Degrees and first jobs change slowly, and they are the part that policy can count: 41.8 percent of new bachelor's degrees in 2025 went to the most exposed third of fields, against 40.7 percent in 2024, enrolment in those fields has edged up, and young workers' employment in the most exposed jobs, against older workers', is 16 percent below its 2022 level.

bridge.mark: 23% of wages in tasks people bring

items.s: of all the wages paid in the United States go to work on the tasks people bring to AI models, in the usage record the Anthropic Economic Index published in March 2026, against 18 percent in its September 2025 release, and 6 percent go to tasks people hand over to the model entirely, on the June 2026 record.
items.src: Anthropic Economic Index, March 2026; OEWS wages, May 2025
items.more: A task counts once any use of it is published, so this reading measures how widely use spreads across paid work and says nothing about how much of that work the models do. It rose from 18 percent in September 2025 to 23 percent in March 2026 as more tasks appeared in the record. The June 2026 file leaves out tasks below a reporting threshold, so the reading stays on the last release that publishes every task.
items.title: Share of US wages in tasks people bring to AI
items.note: Up from 18% in the September 2025 release.

items.s: is the weight of that use on complex problem solving skills, measured against their share of pay and the most of any skill group, while physical abilities receive 0.3 times their share.
items.more: Each skill group's share of use is set against its share of pay, so a value above one means the group draws more use than its weight in wages. Of the twenty-five groups, the most use falls on complex problem solving skills and the least on physical abilities.
items.title: Where use is concentrated
items.note: Use on complex problem solving skills against their share of pay, the most of any skill group.

items.s: of wages are paid for the tasks that together make up three quarters of all that use, 243 tasks in the June 2026 record, against 1.8 percent in the September 2025 release.
items.src: Anthropic Economic Index, June 2026; OEWS wages, May 2025
items.more: Use is concentrated: 243 tasks account for three quarters of it. Counting only those tasks gives a reading that the reporting threshold cannot move, and its move from 1.8 to 3.1 percent means the work people bring most often now sits in tasks that carry more of the wage bill.
items.title: Wages in the core of use
items.note: The 243 tasks that make up three quarters of all use, up from 1.8%.

bridge.how: Each conversation in the usage record is matched to the O*NET tasks it touches, each task is weighted by the wages paid for it in the latest OEWS release, and the share moves with every usage release, every few months, for the one platform whose record the index reads so far. A task counts as reached when any use of it is published, so the headline comes from the latest release that publishes every task, and the tasks making up three quarters of use are counted in every release alike, since no release leaves any of them out.
bridge.index_line: How much of paid work is in the tasks people bring to AI
bridge.headline: The tasks people bring to AI models account for 23 percent of US wages, and that use is heaviest on complex problem solving skills, at 2.5 times their share of pay.

city.capline: pay 2.9, 6.1 needed; jobs mix 8.1, 6.6 needed; job ads 2.6, 5.4 needed

items.s: standard errors is the largest change in pay across the twenty-five skill groups over the last three years, a fall in the pay of mental processes, where 6.1 would be needed to stand out from each group's own record since 2013, and seven of the ten earlier three-year stretches in that record moved as far or further.
items.src: OEWS, May 2012 to May 2025, occupations present in every year
items.more: Each of the twenty-five skill groups is tested against its own changes since 2013, so a group whose pay has always moved a lot needs a larger change to stand out. The test runs again with each spring release of the wage tables, and it measures pay across whole occupations, so a rise for new hires and a fall for people already in the job would largely cancel in it.
items.title: Pay across skill groups
items.note: The biggest three-year move in any skill group is 2.9, where 6.1 would count as unusual.

items.s: standard errors is the largest shift in the mix of skills in employment over the last three years, toward work that draws on arts and humanities, past the 6.6 needed to stand out and further than any of the ten earlier three-year stretches since 2013, although a record of thirteen years produces a shift that size by chance about one time in eleven, and the same test was passed in 2020.
items.src: OEWS, May 2012 to May 2025, occupations present in every year
items.more: The mix of jobs is each skill group's share of employment, so it moves when people move between occupations, which can happen before pay changes at all. It is tested in the same way as pay, against each group's own record, and about one stretch in eleven of a record this long moves this far by chance.
items.title: Mix of jobs
items.note: The biggest shift is 8.1 against 6.6, toward arts and humanities, the largest since 2013; a record this long gives a shift that size about one time in eleven.

items.s: standard errors is the step, at the release of language models, in how much job ads within each occupation ask for the tasks those models can do, measured against the sixteen months before, where 5.4 would be needed to stand out from the same step at each earlier month, and the larger fall came before the release, from 2020 to the third quarter of 2022.
items.src: NLx job ads, September 2015 to September 2025, in the aggregates of Meisenbacher, Nestorov and Norlander; Eloundou task measure
items.more: The aggregates count, for each occupation and month, how many ads name each O*NET task. Within occupations, ads named the tasks the models can do less often from 2020 and reached their lowest point in the third quarter of 2022, so the change in what employers ask for came with the pandemic years and before the technology.
items.title: Job ads for tasks AI can do
items.note: Within occupations, ads named these tasks less often from 2020 to the third quarter of 2022; the step at the release is 2.6 where 5.4 would stand out, and by the third quarter of 2025 ads had made up 68% of the fall.

city.how: For each skill group the index takes the last three yearly changes in pay, and in the share of employment, and sets them against that group's own changes since 2013: a change stands out when it passes the level only the most extreme three-year stretches in the record reached, and both the reading and that level are recalculated with each spring release of the wage tables. The job-ad reading compares, within each occupation and month, the share of ads naming each task with that task's exposure, and sets the change at the release against the same change placed at every earlier month.
city.index_line: Whether pay, the mix of jobs and job ads have moved
city.headline: Pay has stayed within its usual range, the mix of jobs has shifted more than in any three years since 2013, and job ads turned away from the tasks the models can do in 2020 to the third quarter of 2022, before the models were released.

valley.mark: 41.8% of new degrees in exposed fields

items.s: of new bachelor's degrees in 2025 went to the third of fields whose graduates hold the jobs most exposed to AI models, with each field scored by where its graduates actually work, against 40.7 percent in 2024.
items.src: IPEDS completions, 2025; field exposure from ACS and the Eloundou task measure
items.more: Each field of study is scored by the exposure of the jobs its graduates hold in the American Community Survey, so a field counts as exposed because of where its graduates work. The share moves once a year, with each completions file.
items.title: New degrees in exposed fields
items.note: Of bachelor's degrees in 2025, up from 40.7% in 2024.

items.s: of undergraduates at four-year institutions in fall 2024 were enrolled in the third of field families whose graduates hold the most exposed jobs, against 52.4 percent in fall 2019.
items.src: National Student Clearinghouse, Fall 2019 to Fall 2024; field exposure from ACS and the Eloundou task measure
items.more: Enrolment shows the students still in college, three or four years ahead of their degrees, so it is the first place a change in what people choose to study would appear. So far the share in exposed fields has edged up.
items.title: Enrolment in exposed fields
items.note: Of four-year undergraduates in fall 2024, against 52.4% in fall 2019.

items.s: is how far the employment of 22 to 27 year olds in the most exposed third of jobs, set against their employment in other jobs, has fallen since 2022 beyond the same change for workers aged 35 to 54, as of August 2026.
items.src: Current Population Survey, January 2022 to August 2026
items.more: The gauge sets young workers' employment in the most exposed jobs against their employment in other jobs, and divides by the same ratio for workers aged 35 to 54, so it moves only when young workers' place in exposed work changes relative to older workers'. Over the last twelve months it sits 8.4 points below the months before, where reshuffling the months moves it by at most 2.8. The monthly samples are small and the series starts in January 2022, so it does not show whether the fall began before the release of language models.
items.title: Young workers in exposed jobs
items.note: Employment of 22 to 27 year olds in the most exposed jobs, against older workers, since 2022.

valley.how: Degrees come from the IPEDS completions file and enrolment from the Clearinghouse, and each field is scored by the exposure of the occupations its graduates hold, on the task measure of Eloundou and coauthors. Young workers come from the monthly Current Population Survey, with occupations scored the same way. People who move into exposed jobs from other occupations will join this view when the flows between occupations are published.
valley.index_line: What people study, and whether young workers still get exposed jobs
valley.headline: 42 percent of new degrees and 53 percent of four-year enrolment are in fields that lead to the most exposed jobs, while young workers' employment in those jobs, against older workers', is 16 percent below its 2022 level.
